c1.story:
For most of Indian history, owning a Grade-A office building meant being a very rich family, a pension fund in Toronto or a private-equity giant in New York. If you were an ordinary investor who liked the idea of collecting rent from a global bank or a chipmaker, your options were close to none. Then, in 2019, Embassy Office Parks listed on the exchanges, and suddenly you could own a sliver of a Bengaluru tech park for the price of a nice dinner.

That is what a REIT is: a trust that owns finished, rented buildings and is required by SEBI to pay out almost all the cash it collects to its unitholders. An InvIT is its cousin for infrastructure: power lines, toll roads, solar farms. Both trade on the exchange like shares, and both are bought for the payout more than for a story.

But the same yield can mean very different things, and that is the point of the four doors. An office REIT owns a building that will still be standing in fifty years and whose rent can rise every few years as leases renew. A retail REIT, which in India means Nexus Select and its malls, earns fixed rent plus a share of each shop's sales, so it gets a slice of every good shopping season. An infrastructure InvIT is different again. It owns a toll road or a power line under a concession or a tariff order, and when the concession runs out the asset goes back to the government. Part of every payout is therefore your own capital coming back to you.

A REIT pays you rent that can grow. An InvIT often pays you back your own money, slowly, with interest.

The fourth door is new. SEBI created small and medium REITs in 2024 to bring fractional-ownership platforms under regulation, and the Propshare trusts are the first examples: a single building, one or two tenants, and very thin trading. That is a concentrated bet on one address, not a diversified one, and it should be sized like one.
c1.read:
Four tiles, one per door. Read each top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you what the trust owns and how it earns: long leases with rent steps for offices, fixed rent plus a turnover share for malls, regulated tariffs, annuities or tolls for InvITs, and one building with one or two tenants for the small REITs.
  • The tickers are the listed trusts behind each door; click one to open its page. Office has the most names, from Knowledge Realty Trust, the largest, to Embassy, Mindspace and Brookfield. Retail has one, Nexus Select.
  • The profit bar shows how much of the income the trust keeps. Office and retail sit at high: once a tenant has fitted out its floors, moving is expensive, and rent rises at renewal. InvITs sit at medium, because the revenue formula is fixed by a regulator or a contract and the asset has an end date. Small REITs sit at medium, because one empty floor is a big share of the income.
  • The last line is the bet. Notice that the bond appears in two of the four. That is the hidden thread running through all of them: every unit is priced against the government bond.

The analogy below the tiles maps each door onto a landlord, and the so-what line gives the key distinction: office and retail payouts can grow, while most InvIT payouts shrink to zero at the end of a concession. When you compare yields across doors, adjust for that, or you will be comparing a growing rent with a self-liquidating annuity.

c2.story:
A REIT is the last stop on a long journey, and most of the action happens before the trust ever lists.

The journey starts with a builder. In India that has mostly meant global private-equity firms and their local partners. Blackstone, more than anyone, spent the 2010s buying and building tech parks in Bengaluru, Pune, Mumbai and Hyderabad with partners like Embassy, K Raheja and Sattva. Brookfield did the same around Mumbai and the NCR. On the infrastructure side, power developers and firms like KKR built or bought transmission lines and roads. This is the risky part: buying land, getting approvals, building, then finding tenants. Nobody puts a half-empty building into a REIT.

Once the buildings are full, the second station turns them into a listed trust. The sponsor puts the finished, rent-paying assets into a trust, SEBI clears the documents and merchant bankers sell the units in an IPO. The sponsor gets much of its money back and usually keeps a stake, along with the management contract.

The third and fourth stations are the listed trusts' daily job: lease the space, collect the rent or the tariff, maintain the buildings, and then pay at least nine-tenths of the distributable cash out every quarter, as dividends, interest and repayment of debt. Mutual funds, insurers, pension funds and retail investors receive it.

The fifth station is how a trust grows beyond rent increases: it buys more assets, usually from its own sponsor, using fresh debt and new units. This is where the interesting governance question lives. When the seller is also the manager's parent, who makes sure the price is fair?

The trust runs the building. The sponsor decides which buildings the trust gets to run.

And standing beside the whole kitchen is a rival that owns no buildings at all: the government bond. Every investor holding a REIT unit is implicitly asking whether the payout beats a risk-free yield by enough to justify the risk.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, then the band row beneath them, then the rival.

The five boxes follow an asset from construction to payout and then to growth. Under each name you see what happens and who stands there. Notice the shift: global sponsors and developers on the left, regulators and bankers at the listing, the listed trusts in the middle, unitholders at distribution, and sponsors again on the right.

The band row shows who holds each station. Only the third and fourth bands, operating the assets and distribution, are coloured as Indian listed. The first, second and fifth belong to sponsors and SEBI. That is the visual version of the so-what line: the listed trusts do one job, operate and pay out, while the decisions about what gets built and what gets sold into the trust sit with the sponsor.

The rival named here is unusual: not a company but the government bond yield. Think of it as a competitor standing at the distribution station, offering investors a risk-free payout. When the bond yield rises, the rival's offer improves, and unit prices must fall until the trust's yield looks competitive again.

The note under the bands tells you where the office assets sit: the tech-park belts of Bengaluru, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and the NCR, which grew up around IT services firms.

Use the diagram to place news. A sponsor announcing a new park is a station one story that may reach station five in a few years. An RBI rate cut lands on station four through cheaper debt. A big tenant vacating lands on station three.

c3.story:
Walk through a tech park on Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road or in Hyderabad's HITEC City on a weekday and you will see the real customer of India's office REITs. Not only the IT services giants of the 2000s, although they are still there, but the global capability centre: the in-house Indian arm of a Western bank, retailer, chipmaker or insurer, doing work that used to be done in London or Ohio.

GCCs have become the biggest driver of office leasing in India. They sign large floors on long leases, fit them out expensively, and once they have done that they rarely move. A bank that has spent heavily building out a campus in Pune does not leave because a rival park is slightly cheaper. That stickiness is why office REITs keep most of what they earn.

What moves a GCC? Not the Indian economy, mostly. It is the budget decisions of Western head offices, and the case for doing more work in India rather than at home. When US tech firms laid off staff in 2022 and 2023, Indian office leasing slowed and vacancies rose. When the cost case for India came back into focus, leasing hit records. That is why the US earnings season matters to an Embassy unitholder.

The biggest tenant of an Indian office REIT takes its orders from a boardroom in another time zone.

The mall REIT has a domestic customer: retailers and food brands, who pay fixed rent plus a share of their sales. Their fortunes move with urban spending and the shift towards premium brands, and against them stand e-commerce and quick commerce.

The InvITs sell to the state in various forms: grid operators paying for available transmission lines, NHAI and highway users paying annuities or tolls, state distribution companies buying solar power. Their risk is less about demand and more about whether the payer pays on time.

And the final tile is you. The income-seeking investor, comparing a unit's payout with a fixed deposit and a government bond, is the customer who sets the price.
c3.read:
Eight tiles, each a customer group. Read each in three lines: who buys, what they buy, what moves them.

  • The first three tiles, global capability centres, IT services companies, and banks, consultancies and flexible-office operators, are office tenants. Look at what moves them: US and European budgets, IT hiring, return-to-office policies, startup funding. Mostly foreign drivers, which is why office REIT investors read Wall Street's earnings calls.
  • The fourth tile, retailers and food brands, is the mall REIT's customer, moved by urban spending.
  • The next three, the grid, highway users and NHAI, and power buyers, are the InvITs' payers. Their drivers are regulated tariffs, freight, inflation and discom payment discipline: slow, rule-shaped and mostly domestic.
  • The last tile is unlike any other industry's grid: it is the investor who buys the units. Bond yields, deposit rates and tax treatment move this customer, and this customer decides the unit price.

A useful way to use the grid is to sort tiles by what can go wrong. Office tiles fail through vacancy, when a tenant leaves or shrinks. InvIT tiles fail through payment delays or tariff disputes, not vacancy. The investor tile fails through rising yields or a tax change.

The so-what line sums it up: office REITs live on foreign companies' India headcount, InvITs on government payers, and both are priced by someone comparing them with a bond.

c4.story:
A REIT's profit and loss statement is one of the simplest in the market, and also one of the most misread.

Start at the top. Rent comes in from tenants, usually monthly and in advance. The trust pays the costs of running the buildings: security, maintenance, power for common areas, property tax. What is left is net operating income, the cleanest measure of what the assets earn. For a good office portfolio that is most of the rent; for a power line, almost all of the tariff, because a transmission line needs little looking after once it is strung.

Then come the two lines that dwarf everything else: interest and depreciation. Interest is real cash going to the lenders who financed the buildings, and it is the line that moves when the RBI moves. A trust that refinances a large loan at a lower rate puts the saving straight into the next distribution. That is why the rate cuts of 2025 mattered so much to unitholders.

Depreciation is the trickier one. In the accounts it is large, so reported profit looks thin. But for an office park it is largely a bookkeeping charge: the building is not really wearing out at that pace, and a well-located one is often worth more each year. So reported profit understates what the trust can pay. That is why investors ignore earnings per unit and look at distribution per unit.

For a REIT, depreciation is mostly ink. For an InvIT, it is the clock running down on the asset.

For an InvIT, the same line tells the truth. A toll road concession has an end date, and so does the tariff period on many power assets. When it runs out, the asset is gone, and the depreciation charge was simply the accounting for that. So when an InvIT pays more than its profit, part of the payout is your capital coming back. Yield alone tells you little until you know how many years the concession has left.

Finally, net asset value, set by independent valuers. Units trading well below it signal doubt about rents or rates; units near it say the market believes the valuers.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of income down to what is left, for an office REIT and for an infrastructure InvIT. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees of rent or tariff.
  • The input bar is property and asset operating costs. The office REIT spends about a fifth here, the InvIT about a tenth.
  • The opex bar is management fees, insurance and admin, a small slice in both, around a twentieth.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is where the two shapes part. For the office REIT it takes nearly a third. For the InvIT it takes half, because infrastructure trusts carry more debt and depreciate a concession that genuinely runs out.
  • The last bar is what is left: roughly two-fifths for the office REIT and about a third for the InvIT.

Notice how unusual these shapes are compared with almost any other industry on this site: the operating costs are small and the financing and depreciation bar is the biggest bite. That is the picture of an asset-heavy, bond-like business, where the cost of money matters more than the cost of operations. These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any trust's accounts; hover a bar for the amount.

Below the charts, the list marks what matters. Net operating income, distribution per unit, interest and net asset value get a clear yes. Depreciation and capex get a sometimes: depreciation because it is non-cash for offices but real for InvITs, capex because new buildings on spare land are the growth engine. Working capital gets a no; only solar InvITs carry meaningful receivables from discoms.

c5.story:
India's REIT story so far is one full cycle, and an instructive one.

It started brightly. Embassy listed in 2019 to strong demand, and IT hiring was humming. Then, a year later, the world went home. Covid emptied every office park in the country, and for a while the question was not whether rents would rise but whether offices had a future at all. Mindspace and Brookfield still listed in 2020 and 2021, but the mood was grim.

The bust that followed had several layers. Work from home stretched on, especially in IT services. US tech companies laid off staff in 2022 and 2023, slowing GCC leasing. The RBI raised rates, lifting bond yields and making every REIT's payout look less attractive by comparison. Unit prices fell by a fifth or more. Then came a policy problem specific to India: many tech parks sat inside special economic zones, whose rules made it hard to lease vacant floors to domestic tenants, so empty space stayed empty. And the 2023 budget made part of the debt-repayment portion of payouts taxable, cutting the after-tax yield.

The offices were never finished. They were just waiting for a different tenant.

The bottom came in 2023, and the recovery had a clear engine. Global capability centres began leasing space at record pace. Rate hikes ended, and in 2025 the RBI began cutting. SEZ rules were eased so vacant floors could go to domestic tenants. Knowledge Realty Trust, sponsored by Blackstone and Sattva, listed in 2025 as the largest office REIT. And SEBI moved to classify REITs as equity for mutual funds, widening the buyer base.

Today the arrow sits in the boom arc, mid up-cycle. Both legs are working: leasing is strong and rates are lower. The risk from here is not a lack of growth but a reversal of either leg, a rise in bond yields or a slowdown in Western hiring.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top, each labelled with the years of the last cycle: boom in 2019 and 2020, a peak in 2020 as Covid struck, a long bust from 2021 to 2023 and a bottom in 2023. The arrow points into the boom arc, labelled mid up-cycle, with the detail that leasing is strong and rates are falling. Hover an arc to read what defined that phase.

Notice the shape of this cycle. The boom and peak were brief, because the sector was young and Covid cut the first up-leg short. The bust was the long phase. The industry has now spent longer recovering than it did booming the first time.

The timeline runs from 2019, coloured by tone: a boom start, a neutral Covid period, a bust in 2022 and 2023, neutral again in 2024 as leasing recovered, boom in 2025 and the latest entry marked as now.

The four hands are what move the arrow.

  • Office leasing and vacancy: record leasing, vacancy falling, up.
  • Government bond yield: lower than in 2024, marked up because lower yields help unit prices.
  • Rent reversion on renewals: positive, up. Expiring leases are re-signing above old rents.
  • Price to net asset value: near parity, mixed. The market neither doubts the valuers nor gives the trusts a premium to grow by issuing units.

Three hands up and one mixed is the reading of a healthy mid-cycle. Watch the bond yield hand most closely: it is the one that can turn fastest.

c6.story:
If you want to understand why a REIT unit moved today, look first at the bond market, not the property market.

Here is the mechanism. A REIT or InvIT unit is, to most of its buyers, a stream of quarterly payouts. Investors compare that stream with what they could earn risk-free in a government bond. When the bond yield rises, the unit's payout looks less attractive, so its price falls until the unit offers enough of a premium again. When the bond yield falls, the reverse happens. InvITs, whose payouts barely grow, feel this most, much like a long-dated bond. Office REITs feel it too, softened by the prospect of rising rents.

The policy rate is the second three-dot dial, through a different channel. Trusts borrow to buy and build, so their interest bill follows rates with a lag, as loans reset or get refinanced. A rate cut becomes a bigger distribution a quarter or two later. In 2025, as the RBI cut, that channel turned from headwind to tailwind.

The bond yield sets the price of the payout. Office leasing sets its growth.

The third three-dot dial is the growth engine for offices: global tech and GCC spending. When Western companies expand their Indian centres, parks fill and rents rise at renewal. When they freeze hiring, vacancy creeps back. That is why a US tech earnings season can move Mindspace more than an Indian GDP print.

The smaller dials belong to particular doors. Urban consumption lifts mall turnover rents. Wholesale inflation feeds annual toll increases for road InvITs. A weaker rupee makes Indian offices cheaper for foreign tenants. Discom finances decide whether solar InvITs get paid on time. And two policy dials matter for every unitholder: the tax on distributions, which the 2023 change showed can move after-tax yields overnight, and the new equity classification, which lets mutual funds hold REITs as equity.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches the unitholder. Notice that two channels lead to the price of the unit, the bond yield and equity fund flows; one to the cost of debt, the policy rate; and the rest to income: leasing, consumption, tolls, the rupee and discom payments.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts. Three dials are red: the government bond yield, the policy rate and the tax on distributions. Every other dial is green. There is no diamond here; this is an industry where the direction of each force is clear.
  • Weight: one to three dots. Three dots sit on three rows: the bond yield, the policy rate and global tech and GCC spending.

The last column shows today's reading where the dial maps to a series we track: a government bond tracker, the money-market rate, the Nifty IT index as a proxy for tech spending, the FMCG index as a proxy for urban consumption, the rupee and the Nifty. Wholesale inflation, the tax treatment and discom finances show a dash; for those, follow the budget, the toll notifications and state payment data.

Read the three-dot rows first. Two of them are about the price of money and one about the demand for space, which matches the so-what line: if you track only the bond yield and office leasing by global companies, you have both the price and the growth of the payout. Everything else adjusts the picture at the margin.

c7.story:
The bottlenecks in this industry are less about running buildings and more about who controls the pipeline, the calendar and the tax code.

Start with the sponsors. A handful of global private-equity firms, Blackstone above all, along with Brookfield and their partners, built most of India's listed office stock and still sponsor most of the trusts. They decide which assets get sold into the trust and at what price. That is not necessarily bad; a strong sponsor brings a pipeline and expertise. But it means growth arrives on the sponsor's timetable, and every acquisition is a related-party deal that unitholders should read carefully. This one is structural: it is how Indian REITs were born.

The second structural bottleneck belongs to InvITs: concession end dates. A toll road returns to NHAI when the concession ends. The payout from such an asset is part income and part return of capital, and the yield that looks generous today is partly your own money.

Before you read an InvIT's yield, read the date its concessions end.

Then come the recurring ones. Leases signed in the late-2010s boom tend to come up for renewal in clusters. In a strong market, that is an opportunity to reset rents upward; in a weak one, the risk of a big tenant leaving. And tax rules can change with a budget speech, as unitholders learned in 2023 when part of the debt-repayment portion of payouts became taxable.

The slow one is the SEZ problem. Many tech parks sit inside special economic zones, set up when export-oriented IT firms got tax breaks there. Domestic tenants could not easily use that space, so when an exporter left, the floor could stay empty for a long time. The 2025 easing helps, but filling older vacant blocks takes time.

Finally, thin ownership. Most units sit with institutions and small REITs trade rarely, so prices can swing on small flows. That cuts both ways: a forced seller pushes the price down, and a new index or fund buyer can push it up quickly.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck: name, why it bites, and a severity label. The label tells you where to file each risk.

  • Structural: sponsor concentration and concession end dates. Permanent features that belong in your valuation. For an InvIT, the concession date is the single most important fact you need before reading its yield.
  • Slow: SEZ vacancy. It is fixing itself after the 2025 rule change, but at the pace of tenant negotiations and fit-outs.
  • Recurring: lease expiry clusters and tax rule changes. These are the quarter-to-quarter surprises. Check each trust's lease expiry schedule in its investor presentation; a big block expiring in a weak market is a known risk with a known date.
  • Two-sided: thin retail ownership and liquidity, which can push prices too low on a forced sale or too high on a burst of new buying.

Notice that no row is labelled cyclical. The cyclical risks for this sector, rates and leasing, live on the wiring diagram, not here. These bottlenecks are about structure and rules.

The so-what line gives the reading order: sponsor concentration and concession end dates never go away, so price them once; lease expiries and tax changes are what to watch each quarter. For an office REIT, the practical question is which tenants come up for renewal in the next couple of years and at what rent compared with the market. For an InvIT, it is how many years are left on each asset.

c8.story:
REITs exist because of a rulebook, and the rulebook is what makes them work. Take away SEBI's regulations and a REIT is just a property company with an unusual dividend policy.

The core rules are simple and strict. At least nine-tenths of distributable cash must be paid out to unitholders. Most of the assets must be completed and earning income, so the trust cannot gamble the payout on speculative construction. Borrowing is capped. Together these turn a REIT into something an income investor can rely on: a pass-through vehicle for rent.

The rules that stop a REIT from taking risks are the same rules that make it worth owning.

The newer rules are about who can buy. In 2024 SEBI created small and medium REITs, so fractional-ownership platforms that had been selling slices of single buildings to wealthy individuals came under proper regulation. Then SEBI moved to let mutual funds classify REIT units as equity rather than as a hybrid, which matters because equity funds are far larger than hybrid ones. That opens the door to index inclusion, which would bring passive money.

Tax is the rule that bites unitholders most directly. Payouts come in three flavours: dividends, interest and repayment of debt. Each is taxed differently, and since 2023 the debt-repayment portion has been taxable once it exceeds what the investor paid. A trust whose payout leaned heavily on debt repayment looked very different after that budget.

Outside SEBI, several other bodies shape the income. The commerce ministry's SEZ rules decide whether vacant tech-park floors can be leased to domestic tenants. RBI sets the policy rate and lets banks lend to the trusts. CERC tariffs and NHAI's concession agreements set the revenue formula for transmission and road InvITs. And the stock exchanges' index rules will decide whether REIT units ever join the equity indices.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and its status.

  • Always: SEBI's core REIT and InvIT regulations and the CERC and NHAI concession agreements. These are the permanent architecture: the payout rule, the leverage cap, the revenue formula for infrastructure.
  • Live: the small and medium REIT framework, the tax treatment of distributions and RBI. These shape payouts and pricing right now. The tax row is the one to reread at every budget.
  • New: the equity classification for REITs and the eased SEZ rules. Both are recent tailwinds. The first widens the buyer base; the second lets trusts fill floors that used to stay empty.
  • Coming: stock exchange index rules. Index inclusion would bring passive buying, and it is the next question the timeline flags for 2026.

Notice how much of this rulebook is favourable right now. Two new rules are tailwinds and the coming one would be another. The risks sit in the live rows, especially tax, where a single budget line can change the after-tax yield.

When a regulatory headline lands, use the why-you-care column to decide who it hits. A change to the payout rule or leverage cap touches every trust. A tax change hits trusts whose payouts lean on the affected component. An SEZ change matters mainly to office REITs with large SEZ campuses. Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Five forces asks who gets to keep the money once it comes in. For REITs and InvITs, the answer depends on whether you think of the trust as a landlord or as a bond.

As a landlord, an office REIT is in a decent position. Rivalry is real: in every city, unlisted parks owned by developers and other funds compete for each large tenant, and in a weak market they will cut rents to fill floors. But once a tenant has signed and fitted out, it is reluctant to move, which tames buyer power. New Grade-A parks take years and scarce land near the right roads and metro lines, so entry is slow. And suppliers, the people who clean, guard and maintain the buildings, are plentiful.

An InvIT as a landlord is even better placed. A power line or a toll road has no competitor on its route; nobody builds a parallel highway to undercut the toll. The payer is bound by a regulated contract. On the business itself, an InvIT faces less pressure than an office REIT.

Then flip the lens to the investor, and the picture changes. For the person buying units, an InvIT's fixed, self-liquidating payout looks a lot like a bond. So the real substitute for an InvIT is every government bond, corporate bond and fixed deposit in the market. That is the one force where the InvIT scores worse than the office REIT, and it explains why InvIT prices track bond yields so closely.

On the ground an InvIT has no rivals. In the investor's portfolio it has thousands.

Office REITs face a substitute of their own: remote work, which briefly looked existential in 2020 and 2021. It has faded as a threat, but it never quite goes away, and every return-to-office memo from a large tenant is a small vote on it.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: office and retail REITs, and infrastructure InvITs. Both are fairly small, which fits a sector where assets are scarce and tenants sticky. Look at the overall size first: the two are close, but they bulge in different directions.

  • Rivalry: the REIT shape reaches further, two against one, because offices compete with other parks in the same city while a power line or toll road has no rival on its route.
  • Suppliers: both at one. Sponsors hold the pipeline, but services are plentiful.
  • Buyers: the REIT a little higher than the InvIT, because large tenants negotiate hard while InvIT payers are bound by contracts.
  • Entrants: level, both modest.
  • Substitutes: here the shapes cross. The InvIT shape juts out to the biggest score on the chart, because bonds and deposits easily replace an InvIT in a portfolio.

So the REIT shape is wider on the business spokes, and the InvIT shape is longer on the investor spoke. That crossing is the whole story of the card: the InvIT has the better-protected asset and the tougher competition for capital.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. If you own a particular trust, redraw its shape: an office REIT with heavy SEZ exposure might deserve a higher rivalry score, and a road InvIT with a short concession a higher substitutes score.

c10.story:
A REIT results release is long, glossy and full of photographs of atriums. You can skip most of it. Eight numbers do the work.

Start with distribution per unit, the cash that reaches you. For an office REIT you want it growing steadily as rents rise and floors fill; for an InvIT you want it stable and, crucially, you want to know how much of it is interest and dividend and how much is repayment of capital.

Then the occupancy and pricing numbers. Committed occupancy tells you how full the buildings are, including leases signed but not yet started. Rent reversion tells you what happens when an old lease expires: did the tenant re-sign at a higher rent, or did the trust have to cut to keep them? Positive reversion in a market with falling vacancy is the clearest sign of pricing power. Weighted average lease expiry tells you how long the current rent is locked in.

Net operating income growth is the earning power of the assets in one line, rent minus the cost of running them.

Occupancy tells you how full the building is. Reversion tells you how much the tenants want to stay.

Then the balance-sheet numbers that decide how much growth the trust can afford. Net debt to asset value shows how much room it has to borrow before it hits the regulatory cap. The cost of debt shows whether refinancing will lift the payout: if the trust's assets yield comfortably more than it pays its lenders, borrowing to grow adds to distributions; if the gap narrows, it subtracts.

Finally, price to net asset value: the market's verdict on the independent valuers. A deep discount says investors doubt the rents or the rates; a premium lets the trust grow by issuing new units, because each new unit buys more than a rupee of assets.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number: what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of each trust.
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, the only column with figures. Notice that some rows separate offices from malls, or office REITs from InvITs, because the right answer differs by door: growth for one, stability for the other.
  • Today's industry median appears only on the two rows that map to standard filings: net operating income growth, read through revenue growth, and cost of debt, read through interest relative to operating profit. The other six rows, distribution per unit, occupancy, rent reversion, net debt to asset value, price to NAV and lease expiry, come from the trusts' own quarterly presentations and the exchange price, so they show a dash.

One caution: the median blends office REITs, the mall REIT, small REITs and every InvIT in the list, which is a mixed bag. An office REIT should be compared with the office benchmark, not the blended median.

The trick is to read three numbers together for any trust. Occupancy, rent reversion and cost of debt between them tell you whether the payout will grow. Price to NAV tells you what the market already expects. When the first three are improving and the fourth still shows a discount, the market is behind the data; when they are flat and the unit trades at a premium, it is ahead.

c11.story:
The best early signals for India's office REITs come from far outside India. A US bank announcing a new technology hub in Hyderabad. A chipmaker expanding its Bengaluru design centre. A Western retailer's finance chief talking about moving more work offshore. Each of those is a lease being negotiated today that becomes rent a year or so from now.

That is why the furthest-reaching dots on the chart sit two quarters ahead. Office leasing by global capability centres turns into rent only after the tenant finishes its fit-out. US tech earnings and hiring guidance sit at the same distance, because global budgets decide India headcount and therefore space. So does the sponsor pipeline: when a sponsor signals it will sell new assets into the trust, payout growth follows a couple of quarters later.

Closer in, the RBI policy rate speaks one quarter ahead, because a cut lowers interest costs at the next refinancing. Mall tenant sales do the same for turnover rent. And the government bond yield sits at the same quarter, the fastest signal of all: unit prices move with it the same day.

Put it together and you get the three-sign rule: office vacancy falling, bond yields falling, renewals repricing above old rents. Today all three are ticking. That is rare, and it is why the call describes a healthy up-cycle with both legs working. The flip side of three ticks is that there is no sign left to turn on. From here, the question is which tick turns into a cross first.

Three ticks is the best reading the rule can give. It is also the reading with nowhere left to improve.

The likeliest candidate is the bond yield, because it moves fastest and is driven by forces far beyond Indian property. That is why the call treats InvITs as fairly priced bond substitutes after the rate cuts, and leans towards office REITs whose growth comes from leasing and spare land rather than from rates alone.
